#uranium #silver #copper #graphene

UPDATED: My current top picks 👇 October 11, 2026

Several names have reached new milestones, while others are waiting for the next results. With year-end approaching, tax-loss selling could create buying opportunities in some of the harder-hit stocks. I’m watching the underlying projects and balance sheets before treating a lower price as an opportunity.

☢️ URANIUM

Producers & Developers

$CCJ – My blue-chip uranium pick. Cameco is now part of a proposed U.S.–Korea reactor buildout framework involving Westinghouse AP1000 reactors. The agreements still need to be finalized, but its reach across uranium, fuel services and reactors remains the appeal.

$KAP – I still like its production scale and cost position. The next operating update will be important for judging output, production costs and the effect of input prices.

$DNN – Phoenix construction remains the central catalyst. The project is moving through its first-year construction milestones; delivering the freeze wall and keeping costs and schedule on track matter more than ever.

$NXE – Rook I is under construction, while drilling continues to show potential beyond the established resource. Financing the build and executing it at scale remain the decisive tests.

$UUUU – The Australian Strategic Materials acquisition added rare-earth metal and alloy capabilities to its uranium business. Shares have fallen sharply this year; I’m watching whether the combined operations can deliver on the integrated supply-chain plan.

$UEC – Its latest annual results showed production rising as Christensen Ranch and Burke Hollow ramped up. A large liquid-asset position supports the growth plan; sustained production is the next proof point.

Explorers

$SYH – Drilling has begun at Getty East in a Denison-funded program at Russell Lake. I like the combination of flagship exploration and partner-funded work, with assays from this campaign the next thing to watch.

$M.CN – Myriad regained full control of 24 Arizona breccia-pipe prospects, adding another path alongside Copper Mountain. I’m watching for laboratory results and further work that can turn the early indications into defined targets.

🥈 SILVER

Producers

$HL – Lucky Friday’s record output in the last reported quarter remains a reason I hold Hecla among my preferred silver producers. The next operating report needs to show that strength continuing across the business.

$AG – Q3 delivered 3.4M oz of silver, although a 12-day labor disruption at San Dimas affected production. I’m watching for a steady finish to the year and continued resource growth.

$PAAS – An updated reserve estimate put silver reserves at roughly 511M oz. Cash generation and La Colorada Skarn remain the attractions; Q3 results are due in November.

Explorers & Developers

$HYMC – Recent technical work is assessing processing options for Vortex and Brimstone, as well as a possible heap-leach restart. The high-grade exploration story is compelling, but metallurgy and development economics must carry it forward.

$GRSL.V – San Marcial drilling continues to support the case for resource growth. I’m looking for more step-outs and an updated picture of the deposit’s scale.

$JTWO – My wildcard. Sierra Plata’s surface work identified seven veins and strong silver samples. Trenching, permits and eventual drilling are the next tests; surface samples are still early evidence.

🟠 COPPER

$CGNT.V – My primary copper exposure. Mocoa drilling returned another long copper-equivalent intersection, and the company has outlined targets beyond the current resource. Continued drilling and the planned preliminary economic assessment are what I’m watching.

⚫ GRAPHENE

$HG $HGRAF – Still my largest holding. HydroGraph showcased its Fractal Graphene Paste in October and has proposed a U.S. redomicile vote later this month. Texas scale-up and converting customer work into commercial orders remain the catalysts that matter most to me.

📊 YTD share-price performance for all 16 companies in the attached table, through the October 9 close.

Disclosure: I have paid partnerships with Myriad Uranium and Skyharbour Resources.

Not financial advice. Please do your own due diligence.

thread_tweets.text:
I agree. I’ve seen so many kids on X saying $META is going to eat $SNAP for dinner.

But AR and VR are two very different things.

AR (augmented reality) is far more practical for everyday life.

Imagine walking down the street, seeing someone wearing something you like, pointing your glasses at it, and instantly adding it to your shopping cart. AI could even buy it for you.

Or imagine walking past an apartment, looking at it, and instantly seeing its price. Then asking your glasses to show you the prices of all the apartments nearby.

The possibilities are endless. AR could become part of everyday life in a way VR never will.

𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝗜𝘀 𝗢𝗻𝗲 - 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝗼𝗳 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆

𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭. 𝘉𝘶𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘺𝘰𝘶’𝘳𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭. 𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘨𝘨𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘦.

-Tibetan Buddhist teacher

Over the last couple of weeks, I have been exploring a thought experiment that has taken me deeper and deeper into the Self.

The more I observe life, the more waking reality reminds me of a dream.

Of course, dreams and waking life follow different laws. But that is not the point.

Nobody has ever returned from the grave to tell us what happens after death. Yes, there are stories of people who were declared clinically dead and later revived. But perhaps the doctors were mistaken about their condition, or perhaps their hearts had stopped while their brains had not yet suffered irreversible damage. None of this proves that someone has experienced irreversible death and returned.

So, having never experienced death myself, I am left with the closest experience I have: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲.

When we dream, everything feels real. People, animals, trees, love, fear, anger, desire. An entire world exists, and we believe in it completely.

Then we wake up.

Suddenly, we realize that the people, the trees, the animals, and even the person we believed ourselves to be were all made of the same fabric.

𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲.

And perhaps this is the simplest way to understand the ancient idea that 𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝗢𝗻𝗲.

The most fascinating part is that I was no more real than anyone else in my dream. I wasn’t the one real person surrounded by imaginary characters. 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗼𝗼.

Today, walking through the streets of Istanbul, I watched hundreds of people passing by. Different faces, different lives, different desires. Everyone seemingly living inside their own reality.

And I asked myself: 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝗜 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗮 𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺?

I assume these people have their own inner experience, just as I do. But I cannot directly know their awareness, any more than I can know the awareness of characters inside my dreams.

Perhaps the only thing I can know directly is awareness itself. Whether dreaming or awake, experience is happening. Even deep sleep raises the question of whether awareness disappears or simply has nothing to observe.

And this brings me back to the 𝘈𝘴𝘩𝘵𝘢𝘷𝘢𝘬𝘳𝘢 𝘎𝘪𝘵𝘢:

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘴𝘦𝘦𝘳𝘴, 𝘴𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘺𝘰𝘨𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘦 𝘰𝘯 𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘵𝘭𝘦. 𝘚𝘦𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴, 𝘸𝘩𝘰 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘣𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘥𝘪𝘧𝘧𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸𝘭𝘦𝘥𝘨𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘭𝘭?

Imagine realizing, while dreaming, that everything is a dream. Suddenly, the problems, ambitions, victories, and defeats lose their importance. They still exist within the dream, but 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲.

There is nothing left to prove, nothing you must achieve. You can simply become still, observe, and turn inward.

Perhaps waking life is no different.

I don’t know whether reality is a dream. And I don’t need to know. 

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀. It loosens my attachment to the person I believe myself to be and takes me deeper into the Self.

And here is the most important realization:

𝗜𝗳 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺, 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗲𝗹𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗜 𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗮𝗺 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹.

𝗜 𝗮𝗺 𝘂𝗻𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗼𝗼.

My memories, my personality, my ambitions, even the person asking these questions are all part of the same dream.

Just as the dreamer is not the character inside the dream, perhaps I am not the person I believe myself to be.

Perhaps what remains is awareness itself.

𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗵𝗮𝗽𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘀𝗮𝗶𝗱: 𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝗢𝗻𝗲.

tweets.text:
One of my more controversial bets: the AI feed will be the form factor of 2027!

Most people don’t know what to prompt, and they won’t prompt their way into complicated agentic workflows. With chat, we ask users for digital labor: figure out what AI can do, explain the task, provide the context, repeat. That’s a lot to ask if we want billions of people using agents every day. 

Meanwhile, people already spend hours in feeds. Twitter, Instagram, LinkedIn. They know how to scroll, discover something useful, and act on it.

An intelligent system that knows you should bring you the next useful action. Here’s the email you need to answer, already drafted. Here are the latest sales numbers, with an update ready to send to your team. You approve, edit, dismiss, or jump into chat to go deeper. That’s how people will discover what agents can do, without having to invent a prompt first.

And you can put ads in a feed, one of the biggest business models on the internet. A system that understands your plans can recommend a relevant restaurant, product, or service, clearly labeled as sponsored. You get a reason to come back every day, useful work ready to approve, and a business model to fund the agents doing it.

The real SaaS apocalypse is pretty simple: every piece of software becomes reproducible. The cost of building it goes toward zero, competition becomes brutal, and eventually the price follows. Good luck charging for something anyone can recreate.

Computer use is the breakthrough here imo. Here’s how it works:

One agent navigates the existing software, clicks through every feature and documents everything in a markdown file. A swarm of agents builds it. Another agent acts as the verifier, opens the new software, clicks everywhere, checks that everything works, sends bugs back. Repeat.

I think this scenario is very possible and very much in the work. 

But people are missing the other side which is the bull case for big tech cos. 

If you’re Adobe, you already have a massive test suite documenting how the software is supposed to behave, including all the backend stuff you can’t discover by clicking around. You have insane usage telemetry, decades of customer feedback, and you know which obscure features people actually depend on.

You can build the same software factory. Except you start with a huge advantage.

Use the agents to clean up decades of legacy code. Make the software load faster, feel faster, break less. Give it clean APIs that agents can use. Then use your distribution to ship that better product to millions of existing customers.

Even if you burn $1M in tokens doing this, that’s roughly the annual cost of a handful of engineers in the Bay Area.

And getting the mass market to switch takes time. Especially in the enterprise. A free open-source alternative still has to earn trust, build credibility and convince people to move their workflows. “We cloned Photoshop” doesn’t automatically do that.

So there’s also a pretty strong bull case: the incumbents build the software factory first, use their tests, customer knowledge and distribution to move faster, and end up with better software, higher margins, more revenue and happier customers.

If they don’t move fast enough, well, we’re back to the bear case.
